takeaways: Jason talks with Andy of Everest Home Inspections, an inspector since 2016 with a background in new construction and remodeling, about what inspections cover and what repairs cost.

Radon: the state says about 40% of Minnesota homes have high radon levels. The EPA action level is 4 picocuries per liter, and mitigation typically runs about $2,000 to $3,000. Testing takes about two days.

Other inspections: a quick 45-minute major-component walkthrough before writing an offer in a competitive market, a sewer scope (old clay and Orangeburg pipes, root intrusion, even damage on new homes), and a septic inspection for systems over about 20 years old; replacement can run $35,000 to $45,000.
Stucco homes built from about 1990 to 2005 had widespread moisture problems, with repair bids of $175,000 to $400,000 in some cases. Get invasive moisture testing on stucco from that era.

Electrical: fuses are common before about 1960, panel replacements run about $5,000 to $10,000, and removing knob-and-tube wiring can cost $10,000 to $25,000 plus wall repair. Watch for aluminum branch wiring from older eras.

More checks: foundation cracks wider than about 1/16 inch signal real movement; carbon monoxide alarms belong within 10 feet of each bedroom; masonry fireplace repairs can run $5,000 to $10,000; and boilers, furnaces and water heater venting all get a look.

faq.q: How common is radon in Minnesota homes?
faq.a: The state estimates about 40% of Minnesota homes have high radon levels. Testing is inexpensive, and a mitigation system typically costs about $2,000 to $3,000, according to the video.

faq.q: Should I worry about buying a stucco home in Minnesota?
faq.a: Be careful with stucco homes built from about 1990 to 2005, which had widespread moisture problems. Get a specialized stucco moisture test before you buy.

faq.q: What inspections should I get when buying a house in Minnesota?
faq.a: A general home inspection, a radon test and a sewer scope at minimum. Add a septic inspection for homes on septic, and stucco testing for stucco homes from about 1990 to 2005.

takeaways: Jason talks with Jeff, a mortgage lender with about 25 years of experience, about seven ways to raise your credit score before buying. 1: pay on time. Payment history is about 35% of your score; late payments generally reach your report once they're 30 days past due, though late fees start sooner.
Lenders pull all three bureaus (TransUnion, Equifax and Experian) and usually qualify you on the middle score.

2: keep credit card balances under about 30% of their limits; scores dip above 50% and more above 80%. 3: avoid opening new credit while you're getting approved, and don't finance furniture before closing.

4: pay down debt strategically. Conventional loans can allow total debt up to about 50% of gross monthly income and FHA up to about 57%, though about 43% is a comfortable target. A lender's rapid rescore can update scores in days after you pay down specific balances.

5: check your reports for free at AnnualCreditReport.com and dispute errors in writing; bureaus generally must verify or remove disputed items within 30 days. Free monitoring apps can differ from mortgage scores.

6: become an authorized user on a responsible person's longstanding card. 7: keep old accounts open, since closing them can raise your utilization and lower your score. Borrowers without a score may still qualify through manual underwriting or bank-statement loans.

faq.q: What credit score do I need to buy a house?
faq.a: Many FHA programs look for at least about 620, but requirements vary, and some borrowers without a score can qualify through manual underwriting. Talk with a lender about your situation.

faq.q: How can I raise my credit score quickly before applying for a mortgage?
faq.a: Pay credit card balances below about 30% of their limits, avoid new credit, dispute errors, and ask your lender about a rapid rescore after you pay down specific accounts.

faq.q: Should I close old credit cards before buying a house?
faq.a: Usually not. Closing old accounts reduces your available credit and can raise your utilization, which may lower your score. Pay them off and keep them open.
